idiom_name: System.Text.Json JsonConverter<T> (Read/Write), attributes, or an AutoMapper profile
implementation_notes: The translation moves into the serializer: derive from JsonConverter<T>, implement Read(ref Utf8JsonReader) and Write(Utf8JsonWriter), and register the converter through JsonSerializerOptions.Converters or [JsonConverter(typeof(...))], so JsonSerializer applies it automatically; plain renames and shape changes need only [JsonPropertyName]/[JsonIgnore] annotations. For DTO-to-domain translation the dominant library is AutoMapper, where a Profile's CreateMap<Source, Destination>() (plus ForMember for value conversions) declares the mapping and IMapper.Map<Destination>(source) executes it. What replaces the classic structure is that declaration - the Translator class is written by the runtime or generated at startup - and a hand-written translator remains justified for stateful mappings or several wire versions behind one endpoint.
pitfalls: Property matching is case-sensitive by default and GetProperty throws KeyNotFoundException: set PropertyNameCaseInsensitive or use TryGetProperty, otherwise a producer's casing change breaks the consumer.

A converter that leaves the reader unpositioned (not consuming the whole value) corrupts the parse of the enclosing document, and an exception thrown inside a converter aborts the entire serialization - route failures to the invalid-message path.
AutoMapper configuration errors surface at the first Map call, not at startup; run AssertConfigurationIsValid() in tests or unmapped members fail silently in production.
